extracted.intended_audience: Mystery Writers of America members, Edgar Awards chairs and judges, and authors submitting to the Edgar Awards
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and evaluative guidelines governing selection, composition, conduct, and voting of panels that judge submissions for the Edgar Allan Poe Awards (mystery/crime writing). Covers judge eligibility, panel composition, confidentiality, reading practices, and voting rounds/timeline.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Awards Chair responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The General Awards Chair oversees the entire judging process, answers any questions, and resolves any problems; must choose one chairperson for each Edgar category and work with the national board to record new guidelines for future chairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts as overall supervisor of process and custodian of integrity; selects category chairs who in turn form panels. Quoted mission: 'I as the General Awards Chair for 2005 will pay special attention to the integrity of the judging process itself.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Category chair selection and judge appointment
rubrics_metrics.description: Each category chair is chosen by the General Awards Chair and will select four or more other judges to fill out the judging panels (exception: Best Novel usually has eight judges).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panels typically have four or more judges; Best Novel panel is expanded due to volume (over 500 submissions in 2013). Chairs are responsible for assembling a balanced, functioning panel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge eligibility — active status MWA members
rubrics_metrics.description: In all cases, the panels are filled with active status MWA members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are awards given out by working writers to recognize excellence in their field; judges should therefore be active members of MWA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel composition — balanced representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each panel should have a balanced representation of gender and geography, and especially of writers who would normally gravitate to reading one type of mystery over another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balanced panels help ensure every book receives fair consideration across subgenre preferences and demographics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness and impartiality — avoid personal biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Category chairs should choose fair and impartial judges who do not have personal biases against one form of mystery-writing over another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberations should be conducted with the highest level of fairness and open-mindedness to respect the awards' reputation and integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality and nondisclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges are asked to sign a nondisclosure agreement so that all deliberations are kept confidential, both during the judging period and forever afterwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidentiality protects judges from public repercussions and preserves trust among panelists; the decision was motivated by respect and to avoid public disclosures of who voted for whom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give every submission a fair and equal opportunity
rubrics_metrics.description: The panel’s most important goal is to give every book a fair and equal opportunity to impress the judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despite practical reading limits, panels should strive to ensure submissions are not unfairly dismissed and are considered on their merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical reading accommodation — early engagement rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Books that don’t engage within the first fifty pages, for instance, are often put down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizes practical limits on judges' reading time; used as a pragmatic criterion for early triage but panels must still aim for fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ongoing evaluation — personal Top Ten lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout the year, each judge will be starting to compile his or her own personal Top Ten list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges are encouraged to keep in constant communication, compare notes, and make sure every book receives due consideration as lists are formed.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-round voting — panel Top Ten via point system
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal Top Ten lists are compiled in the first round of voting using a simple 10-9-8 etc. point system to establish a final Top Ten list for the entire panel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The point system converts individual rankings into a panel-wide ordered list; this establishes the shortlist for further consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-round voting — produce nominees and winner; tie procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Second-round voting occurs after judges reconsider the final ten selections; this round usually produces the final top five (the Edgar nominees) and the top overall selection (the Edgar winner), although additional rounds may be required to break ties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple rounds allow reconsideration and tie-breaking; panels may conduct further rounds when necessary to reach a final decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeline for voting and announcements
rubrics_metrics.description: Voting is concluded in early January; nominees are announced on or around Edgar Allan Poe’s birthday (January 19th); winners are announced at the Edgar Banquet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides schedule expectations for judges, submitters, and administrators; next year's judges begin work by the time winners are announced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel communication and deliberation conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges are encouraged to keep in constant communication with each other, to compare notes and to make sure that every book receives due consideration; each panel's deliberations should be conducted with confidentiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active communication supports balanced assessment and helps surface works that merit further attention; confidentiality applies during deliberation and afterwards.
